title: Agentic Information Retrieval
blurb: How LLM agents find information — from dense retrieval and RAG to reasoning-intensive retrieval and test-time compute for ranking.

papers.title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering

notes.takeaway: Learns dense bi-encoder embeddings for questions and passages, beating BM25 on open-domain QA retrieval.
notes.why: Established the dense-retrieval paradigm every later neural retriever and RAG system builds on.

papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks

notes.takeaway: Couples a seq2seq generator with a non-parametric DPR index, retrieving passages to condition generation.
notes.why: Named and defined retrieval-augmented generation — the architecture the whole agentic-IR stack extends.

papers.title: Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels

notes.takeaway: Has an LLM write a hypothetical answer document, embeds that, and retrieves real neighbors — with zero relevance labels.
notes.why: First clean proof that LLM generation at query time can replace supervised dense retrieval; a precursor to query-expansion-as-reasoning.

papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey

notes.takeaway: Maps the RAG design space across naive, advanced, and modular paradigms with a retrieval/augmentation/generation taxonomy.
notes.why: The reference map for where any retrieval technique sits inside the RAG pipeline.

papers.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

notes.takeaway: Interleaves chain-of-thought reasoning with tool actions like search, so the model plans, acts, and observes in a loop.
notes.why: The foundational pattern for agentic search: retrieval becomes an action the model decides to take, not a fixed preprocessing step.

papers.title: Interleaving Retrieval with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Knowledge-Intensive Multi-Step Questions

notes.takeaway: Interleaves retrieval with each chain-of-thought step for multi-hop questions, using partial reasoning to drive the next query.
notes.why: Showed multi-hop retrieval must be reasoning-guided and iterative, not single-shot — the seed of reasoning-intensive retrieval.

papers.title: Active Retrieval Augmented Generation

notes.takeaway: Actively decides when to retrieve by watching for low-confidence tokens, then retrieves using the upcoming sentence as the query.
notes.why: Made retrieval timing itself a model decision, closing the gap between 'always retrieve' and 'never retrieve.'

papers.title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection

notes.takeaway: Trains the model to emit reflection tokens that decide when to retrieve and critique whether passages are relevant and supported.
notes.why: Folded retrieval control and self-critique into the model's own decoding — an early test-time-compute-for-retrieval signal.

papers.title: Search-R1: Training LLMs to Reason and Leverage Search Engines with Reinforcement Learning

notes.takeaway: Uses reinforcement learning to train an LLM to interleave reasoning with live search-engine calls, learning when and what to query.
notes.why: Brings the o1/R1-style reasoning-RL recipe to agentic search, optimizing the retrieve-reason loop directly for the answer.

papers.title: MCTS-RAG: Enhancing Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Monte Carlo Tree Search

notes.takeaway: Runs Monte Carlo Tree Search over interleaved reasoning and retrieval steps, letting a small model scale inference-time compute.
notes.why: Shows search-over-reasoning-paths lets small models rival frontier LLMs on knowledge-intensive tasks — a deliberate test-time-compute lever.

papers.title: BRIGHT: A Realistic and Challenging Benchmark for Reasoning-Intensive Retrieval

notes.takeaway: A benchmark where relevance requires reasoning rather than keyword or semantic overlap; standard retrievers score poorly.
notes.why: Defined the yardstick for reasoning-intensive retrieval and exposed how far embeddings alone fall short.

papers.title: ReasonIR: Training Retrievers for Reasoning Tasks

notes.takeaway: First retriever trained specifically for reasoning tasks, via a synthetic pipeline of hard queries and hard negatives; SOTA on BRIGHT.
notes.why: Proves retrievers themselves — not just rerankers — can be trained to reason, and that they exploit test-time compute via richer rewritten queries.

papers.title: RankRAG: Unifying Context Ranking with Retrieval-Augmented Generation in LLMs

notes.takeaway: Instruction-tunes a single LLM to both rank contexts and generate the answer, unifying reranking and generation.
notes.why: Collapsed reranker and generator into one model — a step toward retrieval as a reasoning capability rather than a separate component.

papers.title: A Survey of Reasoning-Intensive Retrieval: Progress and Challenges

notes.takeaway: Systematizes reasoning-intensive retrieval: benchmarks organized by domain, and a taxonomy of where and how reasoning enters the pipeline.
notes.why: The first roadmap of the exact subfield SID-1 sits in, organizing a fragmented, fast-moving area.

papers.title: Rank1: Test-Time Compute for Reranking in Information Retrieval

notes.takeaway: The first reranker trained to spend test-time compute: distills R1/o1 reasoning traces so a small model reasons before scoring relevance.
notes.why: The direct academic statement of SID-1's thesis — explainable, test-time-compute reranking that generalizes out of distribution.

papers.title: Distillation and Refinement of Reasoning in Small Language Models for Document Re-ranking

notes.takeaway: Distills then RL-refines reasoning into a 3B reranker that generates relevance explanations at inference; third on BRIGHT, beating 20x-larger models.
notes.why: Shows the test-time-compute reranking win survives heavy distillation — small, cheap, explainable rerankers that reason.

papers.title: Verbal-R3: Verbal Reranker as the Missing Bridge between Retrieval and Reasoning

notes.takeaway: A verbal reranker that reasons in natural language to bridge retrieval and the generator, instead of injecting raw passages.
notes.why: Positions reasoning-at-rerank as the missing connective tissue of RAG.

papers.title: RICE-PO: Turning Retrieval Interactions into Credit Signals for Reasoning Agents

notes.takeaway: Critic-free policy optimization that turns retrieval interactions into localized credit signals for latent reasoning steps.
notes.why: Tackles the credit-assignment problem blocking the training of reasoning-based retrieval agents — the next training frontier.

papers.title: GRC: Unifying Reasoning-Driven Generation, Retrieval and Compression

notes.takeaway: Unifies reasoning-driven generation, retrieval, and compression in one LLM, sharing training across embedding and generative tasks.
notes.why: Points toward a single model that retrieves, reasons, and writes — erasing the retriever/generator boundary.

papers.title: Hybrid Retriever Evolution for Multimodal Document Reasoning Agents

notes.takeaway: Makes retrieval orchestration itself the thing that is learned: a task agent chooses per step among BM25, ColBERT, ColPali, and a VLM page-retrieval tool, while an offline meta-agent inspects failed trajectories, probes the same tool environment with executable analysis code, and rewrites the task agent's instructions. The evolved agent gains up to +19.6 points (42.4% to 62.0% on MMLongBench-Doc with Gemini 3.1 Flash) without changing retrievers, tools, or backbone.
notes.why: Pushes this branch's retrieve-as-action idea one level up: not just when to retrieve but which retriever to invoke and how to compose cross-modal evidence, discovered through failure-driven evolution rather than a hardcoded pipeline.

papers.title: WebSwarm: Recursive Multi-Agent Orchestration for Deep-and-Wide Web Search

notes.takeaway: WebSwarm turns web search into evidence-driven recursive delegation: instead of committing to a fixed retrieval plan, each agentic node decides whether to search itself or delegate child nodes as intermediate evidence surfaces new entities and constraints, and reuses trajectory experience distilled from earlier sibling nodes to guide later ones. It consistently beats single-agent ReAct and multi-agent baselines across BrowseComp-Plus, WideSearch, DeepWideSearch, and GISA, with gains such as 10.91 Row F1 and 9.76 Item F1 over ReAct on WideSearch-EN.
notes.why: This branch is about retrieval becoming an action the model chooses and repeats; WebSwarm extends that loop from a single trajectory to a recursively expanding tree of search nodes whose shape is decided by accumulated evidence rather than the initial query.

papers.title: ProjAgent: Procedural Similarity Retrieval for Repository-Level Code Generation

notes.takeaway: ProjAgent is a concrete case of retrieval that surface similarity cannot do: it decomposes a target function into reasoning steps and retrieves repository functions that share the same underlying procedure, using LLM hidden-state projections rather than token or embedding overlap. Its example pair, two input-validation guard clauses in different modules, scores only 0.38 BM25 and 0.59 embedding similarity, and removing the procedural signal cuts REPOCOD Pass@1 from 41.14% to 25.76%.
notes.why: This branch defines the regime where relevance runs through a chain of inference and ordinary embeddings collapse; ProjAgent shows code retrieval falls squarely in it, since procedurally related functions are relevant through shared implementation logic that lexical and dense retrievers miss.

papers.title: Bridge Evidence: Static Retrieval Utility Does Not Predict Causal Utility in Multi-Step Agentic Search

notes.takeaway: Replaying a ReAct agent over 1000 HotpotQA questions and deleting each document it read one at a time (Counterfactual Trajectory Utility, built from answer, next-query, and turn-count deltas) shows static reader utility and causal utility are nearly independent (Spearman rho = -0.026 over 23,322 observations); about 35.7% of read documents are 'bridge documents' that are causally load-bearing yet score useless to a static reader.
notes.why: The agentic search loop is exactly where a document's value shifts from what it says about the current question to what it unlocks for the next query; a bridge document earns its keep by handing the agent a discriminative entity (carried into the next query 4.02x more often than non-discriminative ones) that redirects the search, so optimizing static relevance does not optimize the loop.

papers.title: AISE-Bench: A Full-Cycle Curated Benchmark for Information Seeking on Academic Knowledge Graphs

notes.takeaway: 1,133 annotated QA pairs built from real AMiner user queries over an academic knowledge graph, each carrying a query taxonomy, a full multi-step API trajectory with validated parameters, and an answer with embedded reference links, so planning and execution are scored as first-class objects rather than inferred from the answer. The API library covers entity search, entity detail and entity relationship queries across papers, authors, venues and organizations. Across 14 methods - 6 LLMs, 4 API-using agent frameworks, 2 coding agents, 2 commercial deep-research systems - the strongest, PLAY2PROMPT with Gemini-3-Pro, reaches only 61.04% correctness and 60.9% completeness under LLM judges. GPT-5.2 records the highest Planning Graph Edit Distance and the lowest Execution Success Rate because it plans overly long API paths.
notes.why: The loop only becomes debuggable when the retrieval steps are annotated, and that is what separates this from the paper-centric benchmarks it compares against (PeerQA, ScholarQABench) and from graph benchmarks whose trajectories are synthesized by template or random walk. With planning and execution measured separately, the failure lands on the loop rather than the summarizer: a model can hold a defensible final answer while its API path is longer and less accurate than the annotated one. The residual gap at 61% correctness on real user queries marks how much of agentic search is still parameter filling and API disambiguation rather than reasoning over retrieved text.

papers.title: WorkSurface-Bench: Benchmarking Enterprise Agents on Multi-Surface Knowledge Routing

notes.takeaway: The benchmark isolates the decision an agent makes before it retrieves anything: which kind of knowledge the question requires. Five persona-scoped Workspace-Bench-Lite workspaces are projected onto three surface-native interfaces, a 493-document knowledge base, a 207-view DuckDB table registry, and a 1,438-edge file dependency graph carrying file-depends-on-file, file-supports-output and task-requires-file relations, with procedural SOPs left as task metadata rather than a fourth routable surface. The 1,151 atomic tasks split into 213 document, 279 table, 171 graph and 488 cross-surface questions, and each is scored on four separate axes: Route F1 over selected against required surfaces, Evidence over artifact access, Answer, and Efficiency. Four backbones under six agent settings produce 27,624 retained trajectories with no protocol errors. The headline is that routing and answering come apart: gold-constrained agents reach 98.7 to 99.8 Route F1 while Answer stays at 56.1 to 75.3%. A matched intervention separates the two further, with surface hints improving Answer for three of four models while removing irrelevant tools mainly improves routing and efficiency. Reference answers never come from model free text; table answers are reproduced by executed DuckDB queries, document answers checked against verbatim spans, and graph answers derived from source dependency annotations, screened from 2,000 candidates down to 1,151 and audited by three independent annotators over a 200-task sample that passed all six criteria by majority.
notes.why: This branch is about retrieval ceasing to be a fixed preprocessing step and becoming an action the model chooses. Surface routing is that choice one level above retriever selection: the agent picks a representation, and only then a retriever or query program inside it, which is why the paper distinguishes routing among information types from the tool and API routing that MetaTool, T-Eval and API-Bank measure, and from mmRAG, which covers the same three sources but flattens them into retrievable documents instead of keeping surface-native tools. Scoring the choice separately from the answer is what makes the loop debuggable, and it produces the branch's most load-bearing negative result: near-saturated routing sits alongside answers that are wrong 25 to 44% of the time, so the retrieval decision is no longer where the headroom is. The paper is careful that artifact-level Evidence does not prove correct semantic use, so high Route plus high Evidence with low Answer only points at downstream synthesis rather than proving it.

papers.title: EMBL AI Librarian: Life-Sciences Knowledge Layer for AI Agents

notes.takeaway: Librarian puts the retrieve-reason loop inside the knowledge layer instead of leaving it to every agent that needs the literature. A single LLM controller takes a natural-language question, plans complementary keyword and fielded queries against Europe PMC's live search, retrieves the matching records, decomposes the selected papers into paragraphs, scores those paragraphs against the original question, and returns a compact ranked set of citable evidence with source metadata. The loop exists because of a specific property of the corpus: biological entities carry multiple aliases across gene symbols, protein names, disease synonyms and MeSH terms, so comprehensive retrieval requires several complementary searches rather than one good query, and Europe PMC's 11.9M full-text articles and 40.7M abstracts are returned as whole documents ranked lexically, of which only a fraction is relevant. Reading those documents is what consumes an agent's context window. On ScholarQA-Bench the layer improves Citation F1 by more than 16 points over strong recent baselines; used as the retrieval layer of an existing claim-verification pipeline it raises agreement with expert consensus; and on open-form LitQA2 a GPT-5.4 agent scores about 8 points higher grounded in Librarian than with web search. The system is model-agnostic, so a stronger controller upgrades the whole layer.
notes.why: The branch's thesis is that retrieval becomes an action the model chooses rather than a fixed preprocessing step, and this is that thesis packaged as shared infrastructure: the loop is factored out one level, so the calling agent asks a question and gets evidence, and every downstream agent stops reimplementing query planning against a syntax it has to learn. The evidence-not-documents contract is the load-bearing part. What the loop returns is bounded, citable and attributable, which is what makes it composable into a claim-verification pipeline that was not designed around it. It also makes the case that the interface, not the model, was the bottleneck: the same GPT-5.4 gains about 8 points on LitQA2 purely from what it is handed.

notes.takeaway: The paper is a direct argument against paying for a static embedding index when inference-time reasoning can do the ranking. Librarian maintains no index of its own; it queries Europe PMC's live search and spends LLM calls at request time on query planning and paragraph-level relevance scoring against the question. The authors give four reasons for refusing the dense datastore. It is expensive to build and serve, with OpenScholar's alone at roughly 744 GB. Its margin is narrowing, since a well-tuned BM25 backbone driven by a capable LLM issuing multiple keyword queries now matches or exceeds dense retrieval on scientific benchmarks. Embeddings flatten structured metadata, blocking direct queries over explicit fields such as gene, protein, organism and chemical annotations, which is exactly the structure Europe PMC exposes. And a nearest-neighbour lookup is not inspectable, where a fielded keyword query is. The trade lands: more than 16 points of Citation F1 over strong recent baselines on ScholarQA-Bench, higher expert-consensus agreement as a drop-in retrieval layer, and about 8 points on LitQA2 over web search.
notes.why: The branch collects the case for reasoning about relevance rather than embedding it, and this is that case argued on cost and on freshness rather than on accuracy alone. Because ranking happens at query time, the corpus is whatever the live search returns, so there is no index-refresh problem and no staleness window, and the operational commitment shrinks from hundreds of gigabytes of embeddings to LLM calls that scale with traffic instead of with corpus size. The inspectability point deserves carrying into any reranker discussion: a fielded query is a stated hypothesis about what would answer the question, which can be read and corrected, and a vector neighbourhood is not.

papers.title: Diagnosing Search Behavior and Failure Modes in Long-Horizon Search Agents

notes.takeaway: A trajectory-level audit of what the retrieve-reason loop actually buys, run with the retriever and harness held fixed so behavioral differences cannot hide in setup. Six agents (gpt-oss-120b, Tongyi-DeepResearch, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Deepseek V4 Pro, Kimi K2.6, GLM 5.1) run the same ReAct loop over BrowseComp-Plus, whose 830 questions carry human document-level relevance judgments, so every step can be scored against gold evidence rather than an LLM judge. Effort does not track accuracy: search volume runs the wrong way at Spearman rho = -0.77, and the weakest agent issues the most searches. Cumulative gold recall tracks accuracy instead. Failures split into a retrieval gap (evidence never surfaced) and a utilization gap (surfaced, answer still wrong), and the split is not implied by the score -- Kimi K2.6 and Deepseek V4 Pro sit within a point of each other in accuracy on opposite sides of it, so equal leaderboard positions call for opposite fixes. Because all six share one retriever at top-K=5 yet spread 52.0% to 78.7% in gold recall, the retrieval gap is query-side, not retriever-side. The episode-level picture is stark: only 6-23% of episodes add new evidence and 77.5-93.6% add none; the median trajectory has 2-3 productive episodes; by roughly 25 episodes every agent is within 4-10 points of its gold-hit plateau. Incorrect trajectories run 1.9-2.9x longer than correct ones yet their last productive step arrives only 0.6-6.7 episodes later, so the extra length is a wasted tail 3.0-6.1x longer -- and since 48-64% of failing runs never surface a gold document at any budget, that tail is rational continuation under failed retrieval, not a broken stopping rule. Redundant re-querying is the cleanest behavioral marker of failure (rho = -0.83; the one genuine offender repeats on 5.0% of moves against 1.5% or below elsewhere), while query style is not decisive -- anchor-then-verify and enumerate-then-check each win and lose a documented case.
notes.why: The branch treats retrieval as an action the model chooses; this paper measures the choices and finds most of them are not paying. Two consequences matter for anyone building the loop. First, the diagnosis has to come before the fix: more search repairs a retrieval gap and does nothing for a utilization gap, and the paper's oracle ladder bounds how much is even reachable -- swapping in a strong reader over the full evidence set lifts 59.5% to 87.5%, leaving 12.5% hard utilization failure that no retrieval change touches. Second, the loop's real cost centre is not where it looks. Accumulated search snippets fill 66-85% of the context budget while visited documents take only 2-16%, so visit gating buys precision but little headroom, and the lever is upstream snippet management -- deduplication, top-K trimming, aging out snippets whose evidence is already integrated. The prescriptions split by diagnosis rather than by leaderboard rank: reformulate queries when the trajectory saturates without gold, stop on evidence sufficiency rather than a fixed step budget, and shift the strongest agents' effort to verification, where one already sits near the oracle-reader ceiling. A free win sits alongside them -- 18-20% of the wrong answers from the three strongest agents differ from gold only in casing, punctuation, or markdown wrapping, recoverable by normalization without touching search or reasoning.

papers.title: When Deep Research Agents Stagnate: Enhancing Reasoning with Retrieval-Aware Agent Control

notes.takeaway: Analyzing reasoning trajectories of deep research agents shows most iterations contribute little or no improvement to the final answer, because agents lack awareness of their own trajectory and so can't tell when to change strategy or stop. The proposed Retrieval-Aware Agent Controller adds unsupervised search-novelty and information-coverage signals to pick the next action, cutting search calls by an average of 14 while improving the best DRA's accuracy by up to 10% (3% average) on BrowseComp-Plus.
notes.why: A direct instance of retrieval becoming a controlled action rather than fixed preprocessing — trajectory-awareness signals (novelty, coverage) let the agent decide when the retrieve-reason loop has stopped paying off, the exact question this branch tracks.

papers.title: Clarify-Then-Search: A Clarification Benchmark for Deep Search with End-to-End Nugget Restoration

notes.takeaway: 518 pairs built from real Baidu queries, each an intent query plus a blurred version with a constraint (time, region, entity scope, criteria) removed. A Clarifier asks k in {1,2,3} questions, a closed-book User Answerer replies only from the hidden intent and returns unknown when the intent does not state the attribute, a Rewriter that never sees the intent produces the rewritten query, and WebDancer runs deep search on it; scoring is weighted nugget recall against a gold set archived from one WebDancer run on the intent query. Every Clarifier beats the 19.43 no-clarification baseline at k=1 with paired-bootstrap 95% CIs strictly above zero, but the User Answerer returns unknown on 60.0-70.1% of single questions, so most interactions elicit no grounded constraint at all. Raising the budget to k=3 works mainly by cutting the all-unknown rate, from 0.618 to 0.189 for GPT.
notes.why: This branch tracks retrieval becoming an action the model chooses rather than fixed preprocessing. Clarify-Then-Search moves that decision one step earlier, to what the agent asks the user before it searches, and scores it by downstream execution instead of question fluency. It also separates a plausible question from a useful one: models ask region-only questions on 14.3-49.8% of turns and those come back unknown 75.0-86.9% of the time, spending clarification budget without changing the rewritten query.

papers.title: Tunable Tool-Call Rates in LLM Agents via Representation Steering

notes.takeaway: Whether an instruction-tuned model calls a tool at all is carried by one linear direction in the residual stream, extracted without training. Propensity is read as the log-probability of the shared tool-call special token at the first generated position, one forward pass per query; queries are ranked by that score and the direction is the difference of residual-stream means between the top and bottom quantiles, taken in a three-tool harness (search, calculator, Python) so the split reflects calling anything rather than one tool. Adding alpha*v at a mid-late decoder layer (L22 on Qwen3-4B) moves the call rate monotonically from near 0 to 0.79-1.0 across all three single-tool environments, with calls staying well-formed until alpha=+3. On PopQA with live search, the sweep traces a cost/accuracy Pareto frontier: 0.29 accuracy at zero searches rises to 0.56 at about 1.1 searches per question, and 0.58 when combined with a search-heavy prompt. Across five models spanning dense, MoE and multimodal, baseline call rates span 0.07 to 0.83, alpha=-2 drives every one to 0.00, and each frontier rises from 0.18-0.34 to 0.44-0.52 at 0.75-1.2 searches. A direction extracted from three tools suppresses six held-out tools (translation, weather, unit conversion, e-mail, SQL, stock price) more strongly than each tool's own direction for five of the six, and steering changes whether a call happens while task-appropriate routing is preserved (at alpha=+2, PopQA to search 100%, GSM8K to calculator 99%, code to Python 90%).
notes.why: This branch treats retrieval as an action the model chooses, and the usual levers on that choice are fine-tuning, retrieval-supervision, or prompt rewriting. This makes when-to-retrieve a continuous inference-time dial with no training and no prompt change, and shows the dial is knowledge-selective: with positive steering the induced search calls concentrate on the low-popularity PopQA entities the model cannot answer from parametric memory rather than on the popular head. It also separates whether-to-call from which-tool, which are usually measured together, and gives the decision a location in the network - control is inert below L7, strongest and monotone at L21-24, and large but non-monotone above the band, consistent with the decision being computed at mid-late depth.

sections.label: Dense retrieval & RAG foundations
sections.summary: Before agents could search, retrieval had to go neural. This theme is the substrate: dense bi-encoders that beat keyword search, the RAG architecture that bolts a retriever onto a generator, and the first hint that LLM generation at query time can stand in for supervised retrieval.
themes: Dense embeddings replace sparse term-matching for open-domain retrieval (DPR).
Retrieval-augmented generation names the pattern: a non-parametric index conditions a parametric generator (RAG).
LLM-generated hypothetical documents can drive retrieval with zero relevance labels (HyDE) — the first crack of reasoning into the query.

sections.label: Agentic search loops
sections.summary: Retrieval stops being a fixed preprocessing step and becomes an action the model chooses. The model reasons, decides when and what to retrieve, reads the result, and repeats — culminating in RL-trained agents that optimize the whole retrieve-reason loop for the final answer.
themes: Interleave reasoning and acting so search is a decided action, not a fixed stage (ReAct, IRCoT).
Let the model control retrieval timing and self-critique what it gets back (FLARE, Self-RAG).
Train the loop directly with RL or tree search to scale inference-time compute (Search-R1, MCTS-RAG).

sections.label: Reasoning-intensive retrieval
sections.summary: Some queries are relevant only through a chain of inference, not surface similarity — and ordinary embeddings collapse on them. This theme defines that regime, builds retrievers and rankers trained to reason, and maps the fast-moving subfield as a whole.
themes: A benchmark where relevance is mediated by reasoning, not keyword/semantic overlap (BRIGHT).
Retrievers and unified rank-and-generate models trained for reasoning, not just factoid lookup (ReasonIR, RankRAG).
A taxonomy of where and how reasoning enters the retrieval pipeline (RIR survey).

sections.label: Test-time compute for ranking
sections.summary: The SID-1 thesis as a literature: spend inference-time reasoning to judge relevance, rather than leaning on a static embedding. Rerankers that think before they score, distilled small models that still reason, and the training frontier of crediting the reasoning steps inside a retrieve-reason agent.
themes: A reranker trained to use test-time compute, distilling o1/R1 reasoning traces (Rank1).
The win survives heavy distillation: a 3B reranker that explains relevance beats 20x-larger models (InteRank).
Verbal reasoning as the bridge between retrieval and generation, and unifying retrieve-reason-write in one model (Verbal-R3, GRC).
gaps: No one routes test-time compute by how reasoning-intensive a query actually is — compute is spent uniformly.
Credit assignment for the latent reasoning steps of a retrieve-reason agent is barely solved (RICE-PO is an opening move).
Reasoning-intensive retrieval is still English, text-only — multimodal, code, and scientific regimes lack benchmarks and trained retrievers.

reading: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain QA
Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLMs: A Survey
MCTS-RAG: RAG with Monte Carlo Tree Search
InteRank: Distilling Reasoning into a 3B Reranker
Verbal-R3: Verbal Reranker as the Bridge
RICE-PO: Credit Signals for Reasoning Agents
opportunities: Rank1 and ReasonIR show reasoning lifts retrieval, but compute is spent uniformly. A controller that detects when relevance is inferential — and only then spends reasoning tokens — would make test-time-compute retrieval economical at scale.
Credit assignment for latent reasoning in retrieve-reason agents

RICE-PO opens this: in an agent that reasons, queries, reads, and re-queries, only the executable actions are directly rewardable. Training the latent reasoning steps that shape retrieval success is largely unsolved.

BRIGHT and its successors are English and text-only. Multimodal, code, and scientific-literature retrieval — where relevance is deeply inferential — lack both benchmarks and retrievers trained to reason over them.

GRC and RankRAG hint at one model that retrieves, ranks, and writes. The latency, cost, and quality tradeoffs versus a separate dense index plus reranker are unmeasured — and decide whether the boundary should exist at all.
Reasoning chains as a first-class evidence surface

A test-time-compute reranker produces an explicit relevance rationale for every result. Almost no system exposes these to the user or feeds them to the downstream generator as grounded evidence rather than discarding them.
